title: Does Mind-Wandering Harm Learning?
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson reviews a study of 8-9 year olds listening to stories, interrupted periodically to report whether they were focused, distracted by unrelated thoughts, thinking about their own interest or ability, or distracted by the environment. Students who mind-wandered remembered significantly less, both immediately and a week later, undercutting the 'uplifting' theory that mind-wandering helps students make fresh connections. Critically, a student's stated interest in the topic did not protect them from the costs of mind-wandering, and students in the study lost focus roughly 25% of the time. Watson draws out classroom implications: reduce distractions, check for understanding more frequently than feels necessary, and don't assume intrinsically interesting content is immune to mind-wandering -- a caution he extends to his own thinking as well as students'.
points: The core finding: students who reported more mind-wandering remembered less material, both immediately after a story and again a week later, ruling out the possibility that short-term costs wash out over time.
Interest in the content did not protect against the costs of mind-wandering -- 'even the students who REALLY LIKE DINOS didn't learn as much if they mind-wandered.'
Students in the study lost focus roughly 25% of the time, split across unrelated thoughts, self-referential thoughts about ability, and environmental distraction -- a hard cap on what they can learn.
Watson's practical takeaways: reduce classroom distractions, check for understanding more often than feels necessary, and don't assume intrinsically interesting content is immune to mind-wandering.
quotes: First: unsurprisingly (to me), students who mind-wandered remembered less. And, crucially, they remembered less both right away and AND a week later.
Second: surprisingly (to me), the students' interest level didn't matter. That is: even the students who REALLY LIKE DINOS didn't learn as much if they mind-wandered.
Third: horrifyingly (to me), students lose focus roughly 25% of the time.
If we want students to learn 100% of the material, and they’re mentally elsewhere for 25% of the time…well, that distraction puts a firm cap on what they can learn.
Second: check for understanding even more frequently than we might think necessary. Doing so will a) help us know if they are mind-wandering, and b) help keep them focused.
